source: Energy gives the speed at the top of a loop; the circle's force equation gives the push of the track.
Students treat the normal force at the top of a loop as pointing up, or leave out gravity in the centripetal sum.

A loop puts two ideas together: energy gives the speed at the top, and the circle's force equation from Vertical Circles gives how hard the track pushes. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Energy from the release height to the top of the loop ($2r$ up): $$mgh = mg(2r) + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2.$$ At the top both the push $N$ and gravity point down, to the center: $$\role[normal force]{force}{N} + \role{mass}{m}\role[acceleration of gravity]{acceleration}{g} = \frac{\role{mass}{m}\role[speed at the top]{velocity}{v}^2}{\role[loop radius]{position}{r}}.$$ Just making it round means $N = 0$, which needs $h = \tfrac{5}{2}r$.
The object is slowest at the top of the loop. There the track and gravity both pull it toward the center.
A $0.2\ \text{kg}$ block is released from $1.4\ \text{m}$ on a smooth track with a loop of radius $0.4\ \text{m}$. Find (1) its speed at the top and (2) the track's push there.
Writing $N - mg = mv^2/r$ at the top, as if the track pushed up. At the top of a loop the track is above the object and pushes down. Check: with $N = 0$ the equation must reduce to $mg = mv^2/r$.
